Auna is a Peruvian a vertical integrated healthcare (insurer and provider) company with significant potential to capture TAM in Mexico and Colombia, as the success of its business model has already been demonstrated in Peru. Auna is a network of clinical services that includes oncology services (Oncosalud), consultations, surgeries, and healthcare membership plans. It operates around 31 total facilities, 2.3k beds and 1.5M healthcare plans. Around Peru, it has 6 main clinics, in Colombia, it has around 8 centers (1.1k beds), and in Mexico, 3. The rest are medical centers around these countries. This network enables patients to receive medical care in different parts of Peru and LATAM.

Because its business model differs from traditional private hospitals (vertical integrated model, Oncosalud sells plans and Auna attends patients), Auna's network makes it unique. Its closest competitors are Brazilian and Mexican, and if we value the company using comparable multiples, there is significant upside potential for Auna. For any refutating this, the valuation for FCF is also solid (even excluding 2Q26 that was a one time supplier financing)

There are two main catalysts for Auna:

Torre Treca: This is a Peruvian government facility that has been ceded to Auna following a contract that was disputed for several years. This represents potential revenue with zero or minimal CapEx required for remodeling.

Recovery of operations in Mexico and Colombia: Disagreements with suppliers (doctors), lose of volume, mix of contracts, talent overhaul, payers, and government clients caused the company to lose money during the first years they were established there. Now, with more experience in these geographies, they are showing signs of recovery. Once these markets mature, EBITDA and profit could increase significantly.

LEN trades at a discount during the down-cycle, with margins compressed by buyer incentives and mortgage-rate buydowns and ASP declining — pressures that are cyclical and consistent with peak pessimism. A structural undersupply of housing in the US underpins long-term demand. As the #2 homebuilder by scale, LEN would capture a disproportionate share of the volume-×-margin rebound once mortgage rates ease. The thesis buys the normalized earnings power, not the depressed current level.

Valuation is anchored to a normalized mid-cycle EPS (recovered volume × normalized margin), not to the depressed current level, applying a mid-cycle homebuilder multiple of ~10x. The return is generated by the E, not by multiple expansion — the current multiple would compress toward 10x, so the entire lift must come from the earnings recovery. The normalized margin is set below the pre-spin level (~10–11%, not the historical ~13%) to embed the permanent land-cost penalty: the asset-light model raised the cost of capital on land from roughly WACC (~7%) to the ~10% charged by land banks, some ~300bps of permanent margin drag. No ACOR add-back is applied, because at mid-cycle the deferral distortion has already self-cancelled — fees paid approximate fees recognized in COGS once the pipeline stops growing.

LEN is a capital-return machine, with high payout ratios and a history of aggressive buybacks against a modest equity base. ACOR (accumulated option costs on real estate) is the stream of fees LEN pays to keep its land options alive: the fees accumulate on the balance sheet rather than hitting expense immediately, and only convert to cost when the home is delivered and sold. Once that fee drain reaches equilibrium (~FY27–28) and ACOR stops building, free cash flow would inflect positive and fund buybacks that are accretive at depressed prices.

The trough keeps deepening with no visible inflection. If unit orders begin falling yoy for several consecutive Qs, the volume support breaks and the setup shifts from a cyclical trough to structural demand erosion driven by affordability.

"Normal" proves worse than assumed, if incentives are structural rather than cyclical, if the land-cost penalty exceeds ~300bps, or if mid-cycle volume never returns to prior levels because affordability has permanently eroded.

The engine currently runs in reverse, with cash falling, net debt rising, and payouts funded from the balance sheet rather than from FCF. The thesis fails if ACOR equilibrium takes longer than FY27–28, or the cycle forces abandonment of land options, an irreversible cash loss, unlike the reversible non-cash impairments of the land-ownership previous model.

What is being bought is a 113-year-old ultra-luxury brand at trough volumes, with most of the value owed to creditors. At 34.56p (£0.3456; the LSE quote is in pence) and 1,009.6M shares, the market cap is £349M, sitting on £1,545M of net debt at H1 2026 (company definition, including £90M of leases and £39M of inventory financing). EV is about £1.89bn: 10.9x LTM adjusted EBITDA of £174M and 1.3x LTM revenue of £1,432M. The product range has been renewed (Vantage, DB12, Vanquish and DBX, now with S derivatives), and the Valhalla supercar is delivering: about 225 units in H1 2026 and around 500 guided for FY2026. Core volumes are still weak. Core wholesales were 5,266 in FY2025 against 5,812 in FY2024, and core ASP fell 5% in H1 2026 to £182k because of dealer support to clear aged stock.

The valuation uses EV/EBITDA on normalized FY2029E volumes rather than on Valhalla-inflated FY2026 figures, because Valhalla is a limited run that ends. Base: 5,700 core units at £205k, 220 Specials at about £1.0M wholesale ASP, and £150M of parts and other revenue give £1.54bn of revenue. At a 38.5% gross margin and £280M of cash opex, adjusted EBITDA is £312M (20%, against 18.7% in FY2023, the best year on record). At 8.0x, which is where AML traded on adjusted EBITDA in FY2022 to FY2024 and close to Porsche AG today, EV is £2.5bn. The equity is a thin residual. Capex of about £330M a year (a £1.7bn programme for FY2026 to FY2030) plus about £180M of cash interest exceeds EBITDA, so net debt keeps rising unless volumes and margin recover. Each turn of the multiple is worth about £310M, roughly the whole current market cap.

The return does not come from free cash flow, which was -£410M in FY2025 and -£198M in H1 2026. It depends on three things happening in order. First, EBITDA has to close the gap to capex plus interest, about £500M a year. Second, the $1,050M 10.0% and £565M 10.375% senior secured notes due March 2029 have to be refinanced without a debt-for-equity swap. Third, the strategic shareholders have to keep funding the gap: Lawrence Stroll's Yew Tree Consortium (32.99%), Geely (14.08%), PIF (13.88%) and Mercedes-Benz (7.54%), 68.5% combined at FY2025. Their record is to fund it, but at the cost of dilution (shares up about 23% since late 2023) and with related-party transactions attached. The July 2026 £450M HPS term loan was secured on trademarks moved into a new unrestricted subsidiary, and bondholders are threatening to challenge it. The position works as a call option. The base case is worth less than the current price, the bull case is worth about 6x, and the bear case leaves nothing for equity.

FY2026 adjusted EBITDA below £230M (hypothesis: the guidance of an EBIT margin near breakeven and £375-400M of D&A implies roughly £300-350M), or FY2027 core wholesales below 5,000 units. Either means the H1 2026 gross margin gain was Valhalla mix, not recovery in the core business.
Net debt above £1.8bn at any half-year before FY2028, or LTM adjusted EBITDA below £200M at H1 2027. Either one leaves EV at 8x below net debt, so the equity would be worth zero on this frame.

Any one of these breaks the claim: the notes are not refinanced by 31 December 2027; they trade below 60 cents for two consecutive quarters (reported at about 57 cents after the HPS deal, a yield to maturity near 37%); a UK court unwinds or suspends the HPS/Authentic Brands financing; or management proposes an exchange that converts notes into equity.
